title: Tech Bros’ Kids Are Now School-Aged
author: Cassandra Gerdes
summary: Cassandra Gerdes examines a wave of tech-industry founders and venture capital money entering K-12 schooling through microschool chains and AI-driven models, prompted by the collapse of Guidepost Montessori. She structures the piece as the good, the bad and the ugly. The good is urgency and willingness to question that is how it's done, especially for the systems around schools such as scheduling, compliance and parent portals. The bad is the belief that a school can scale like software: curriculum, platform and training can be licensed out, but the teacher-student relationship, classroom culture and community trust must be rebuilt from scratch at every site. The ugly is Guidepost, where venture-fueled growth ended in closures. She argues the best test of a founder is whether they have ever said no to growth.
points: Tech founders' urgency is valuable when aimed at the systems around a school, but harmful when the core of schooling is treated as just another system to disrupt.
Curriculum, platform, brand and teacher training can be licensed and scaled; the teacher-student relationship and community trust cannot be packaged.
Software copies cost nothing and are identical to the original, whereas every new school campus must rebuild its people and culture from zero.
Venture capital and growth-first pressure drove the Guidepost Montessori collapse, leaving families with lost deposits and closed schools.
A practical test for any founder is whether they have chosen to pause growth to protect quality, as SailFuture's Mike Long has.
quotes: The best version of tech bro energy points itself at the systems around the core of a school. The worst version treats the core itself as just another system waiting to be disrupted.

Every one of those four things scales fine. Every one of them can be bought, built once, or licensed out: a curriculum, a platform, a training program are all, by design, things you can hand to a stranger a thousand miles away and expect to work roughly the same.
The heart of a school is its people. The heart of education is the teacher-student relationship, and that relationship is the one thing on this list nobody can package.

It’s an obvious point, but worth spelling out: software scales because copy number ten thousand is not just cheap; it’s identical to copy number one. The marginal cost of the next copy is basically zero, and the quality doesn’t degrade one bit getting there.

But a school isn’t a product you copy. The thing that actually makes a school work – a teacher who knows this specific kid, a classroom culture built by this specific group of adults over years, a community that trusts this leadership team – has to be built again, in full, at every single site, by different people, from scratch.
Name me one education organization – public, private, charter – that scaled to real national size and held its quality constant the whole way there.
The mistake is refusing to be ruthlessly honest about the tradeoff between quality and demand: treating a waitlist as a problem to be solved rather than a signal to be respected.
